passage: Sunday night. Vidya and I finally sat down with a notebook and made three columns: names, rites, children. Names: we each keep our own. Rites: a short ceremony at the temple and a blessing at her church, so both families see themselves in it. Children: they will learn both our festivals and stories, and choose for themselves when they are older. We disagreed about who would speak to whose parents first; Vidya wanted me to speak to hers, and I said I would go with her to both. My mother thinks people will talk. Vidya's father worries about her faith being lost. I am afraid of both conversations, and glad we started before the wedding was booked. It's not that everything is decided. It's that neither of us had to win. Chaitanya

passage:
Amandeep and I have been married eight months, and our first real fight wasn't about money. It was about a baby we don't even have.
Her Nani asked at Gurpurab when we'd do the naming at the gurdwara. My mother asked the same week when we'd do the naamkaran with a pandit. I'm Hrithik, and I just wanted to hide in the car.
That night Amandeep said, "We need to decide this ourselves, before anyone else does." So we sat on the floor with chai and a notebook. We agreed on things one by one: a name that works in both families. Both ceremonies. Both of us at both. Our children will learn both prayers and choose for themselves when they're older.
We showed our mothers the list together. My mother frowned at "both." Her Nani laughed and said, "At least they talk." Honestly, the talking felt more important than any rule we wrote.

qa.q: How long have Hrithik and Amandeep been married?
qa.a: They have been married eight months.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when both families asked about the naming?
qa.a: Hrithik felt anxious and cornered, wanting to hide in the car.

qa.q: What made Amandeep and Hrithik's approach wise?
qa.a: They talked early and decided together, writing down clear agreements on names, ceremonies and upbringing, then showed both families as a team.

qa.q: How does Amandeep's Nani seem to see the couple's list?
qa.a: She seems pleased and reassured, valuing that the couple talks things through.

grounding: An interfaith couple negotiates names, rites and children's upbringing early, facing both families' worry with mutual respect.

passage:
Pre-marriage counselling note, session two.
Jyoti, 25, Christian, and Tarun, 26, Hindu, came in together. Both families have agreed to the wedding, but each mother has sent a list of "non-negotiables."
Today they worked on three topics: the ceremony, future children's names, and festivals. Jyoti wanted a church blessing; Tarun's mother wants saat phere. Tarun said, "Why not both, on different days?" Jyoti agreed, then paused: "But I don't want our kids to feel they have to pick a side."
They argued gently about baptism. Neither tried to win. Tarun said, "Can we decide that when we're parents, together, not now to please anyone?" Jyoti nodded, visibly relieved.
Next step: I asked each to write down which of their mother's items truly matter to them personally, and to bring the list next week.

qa.q: What did Tarun's mother want for the ceremony?
qa.a: Tarun's mother wants saat phere.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti seem relieved?
qa.a: Jyoti felt relieved because Tarun suggested deciding about baptism together later, as parents, rather than to please anyone now.

qa.q: What does the couple's approach do well?
qa.a: They talk early and gently, look for ways to include both traditions, and avoid trying to win any single rule.

qa.q: How might the mothers' lists affect the couple?
qa.a: The lists may put pressure on Jyoti and Tarun and make them feel caught between their families and each other.

grounding: A counselling note shows an interfaith couple working through rites, names and children's upbringing early, with mutual respect over winning.

passage:
Tuesday
Tenzin's parents came to dinner with Ma and Papa tonight. First time both families in one room.
Tenzin's mother brought butter lamps as a gift. Ma had put a Ganesh idol by the door and then, at the last minute, a small Buddha beside it. I nearly cried.
Everything was fine until Papa asked what religion "the children" would follow. Tenzin and I aren't even married yet! His father went quiet.
Tenzin answered: "We've talked about it. Our children will learn both, the gompa and the temple, and decide for themselves." We had talked, three long nights, so I could nod and mean it.
Papa said, "That's very modern." Not happy. Not angry. Tenzin's father said, "It's sensible."
Driving back, Tenzin said, "One rule at a time." I think we'll be okay.
Trisha

qa.q: What did Tenzin's mother bring as a gift?
qa.a: Tenzin's mother brought butter lamps as a gift.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel when Ma placed a small Buddha beside the Ganesh idol?
qa.a: Trisha felt so moved and grateful that she nearly cried.

qa.q: Why did it help that the couple had already talked for three nights?
qa.a: Because they had agreed early, Tenzin could answer calmly and Trisha could nod and mean it, which showed both families a united, respectful plan.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's father have felt when Papa asked about the children?
qa.a: He went quiet, so he may have felt uneasy or worried, but he then called the couple's plan sensible.

grounding: An interfaith couple faces both families' worry about children's upbringing and shows that early talks and mutual respect matter more than any single rule.
